text.title: EARS Requirements Core Rules
text.summary: Eight testable rules. R1-R4 are the grammar. R5 is the trap that no regex closes. R6 is the composition rule with sdd/spec-requirements. R7 routes what EARS must refuse. R8 is the limit that every claim about this methodology has to respect.

rule.statement: Every requirement statement MUST parse as exactly one of five patterns, used verbatim with no renamed keywords and no local dialect: ubiquitous `The <system name> shall <system response>`; state-driven `While <precondition(s)>, the <system name> shall <system response>`; event-driven `When <trigger>, the <system name> shall <system response>`; optional-feature `Where <feature is included>, the <system name> shall <system response>`; unwanted-behaviour `If <trigger>, then the <system name> shall <system response>`. A statement combining two or more condition keywords is the Complex pattern and is legal. Anything else fails classification and MUST be rewritten or explicitly opted out under r6.

rationale.source: Mavin, alistairmavin.com/ears/ — EARS Official Guide, fetched 2026-08-03; templates cross-checked against Wikipedia and Terzakis (Intel, ICCGI 2013 tutorial, 2013-07-21)

rule.rationale: The five templates have been unchanged since IEEE RE'09 (2009). The Rolls-Royce airworthiness case study that produced them reported a reduction in all eight of its identified natural-language requirement problem classes — ambiguity, vagueness, complexity, omission, duplication, wordiness, inappropriate implementation, untestability — after rewriting in EARS. The entire value is that it is a 17-year-old notation other people already know; a faion dialect forfeits that and buys nothing. `If` is the only pattern carrying a second obligatory keyword (`then`), and that asymmetry is the cheapest disambiguator the parser gets for free.

rule.statement: Condition clauses MUST appear in the order `Where` ≺ `While`/`During` ≺ `When` ≺ `If`/`Then`, followed by `the <system name> shall <system response>`. Rank assignment: where=0, while=1, during=1, when=2, if=3; the rank sequence across a statement MUST be non-decreasing. Cardinality: at most one `where`, zero-or-many `while`, at most one `when`, at most one `if` (which REQUIRES a matching `then` immediately before the actor), exactly one system name, one-or-many system responses. A condition keyword appearing AFTER the actor is an ordering violation, not a stylistic choice.

rationale.source: derived — Mavin official guide (`While … when …`) + Terzakis ICCGI 2013 examples (`Where … when …`, `When … if … then …`), both fetched 2026-08-03

rule.rationale: EARS states that clauses "always appear in the same order" but no primary source prints a single total ordering of all four keywords. This total order is the unique ordering consistent with all three sourced complex examples. It is published as DERIVED, not quoted: if a primary source contradicts the `Where ≺ While` edge, only that one comparison moves and only rule E005 changes. Terzakis's own event-driven template — an unmarked, uncommaed precondition trailing the trigger — is rejected because it cannot be machine-separated from the trigger; Mavin is the author and his form is the parseable one.

rule.statement: A statement MUST contain exactly one `shall`. Two `shall` tokens on one line is two requirements and MUST be split into two identifiers. A compound system response joined by `and` / `or` MUST be split unless the two halves share the same acceptance criterion and the same verification method.

rationale.source: Mavin et al. RE'09 problem taxonomy — complexity and duplication classes; linter rule E002

rule.rationale: This is the highest-yield check in the rule set: it is cheap, has no false-positive mode, and it catches the failure a non-technical author actually makes. Watching a founder write requirements, they do not struggle with `While` versus `When` — they write two requirements in one sentence and then cannot say which half failed. `and` inside a CONDITION is legal boolean composition and MUST NOT be flagged; the rule applies to the response only, which is why the parser splits condition from response before linting.

rule.statement: The system name MUST be a named component (`the billing service`, `the checkout page`, `the auth service`), never a bare `the system` / `the software` / `the app` / `the platform` / `it`. The subject of `shall` MUST be the system, never a human role: EARS constrains the system's obligations, and `the user shall …` is grammatically valid and semantically wrong. A prohibition MUST be restated as a positive system response (`shall reject every charge request`), because `shall not` has no test.

rationale.source: linter rules W111 / E003; Terzakis ICCGI 2013 on missing actors

rule.rationale: A requirement whose actor is "the system" is legal EARS and useless traceability: nothing links it to a component, a test file or an owner. Passive constructions (`Data is backed up regularly`) hide the actor entirely, so no one is responsible and no test knows what to call. Naming the component is the single edit that converts a requirement into something a test file can be named after.

rule.statement: `When` marks an expected event on the happy path; `If` marks an undesired condition you would rather never occurred. Both forms parse, so the distinction is NOT syntactically detectable and the linter's vocabulary heuristics (W106, W107) MUST remain warnings forever and MUST NOT be promoted to errors. Where `user-flows.md` exists, the keyword MUST be GENERATED from it — happy path → `When`, negative path → `If … then`, precondition → `While` — rather than detected after the fact.
rule.rationale: This is the single most common EARS error. Detection is a lossy vocabulary heuristic; generation is exact, because `user-flows.md` already separates "Happy path" from "Negative paths" and that split IS the `When`/`If` distinction with the keywords removed. A generator reading that file emits the right keyword with no inference. Building a better regex here is the wrong engineering: the information exists upstream and is being thrown away.

rule.statement: EARS composes; it neither replaces nor competes. `sdd/spec-requirements` owns identity and metadata; EARS owns exactly one field — the statement sentence. (1) Every requirement keeps its `FR-NNN`/`NFR-NNN` id, `priority`, `verification_method` and traceability, unchanged. (2) The sentence after the id MUST parse as one of the five patterns (or Complex) for **every `FR-NNN`**. No exceptions. (3) For **`NFR-NNN`** it MUST parse where the requirement is a system response to a condition; where it is not (architectural constraints, quality attributes) it carries `ears_pattern: n-a` plus a one-line reason — explicit and recorded, never silent. (4) Never an EARS sentence without an `FR-NNN`; never an `FR-NNN` without a parsing statement or a recorded `n-a`. (5) `spec-requirements` rule `r5-no-vague-language` (`fast, easy, simple, robust, scalable`) is superseded by W103/W104/W108/W112, a strict superset with a citation per token; the inline list is deleted and points at `templates/ears-rules.json`. (6) `verification_method` is *suggested* from `ears_pattern` — event → integration, state → state-machine, unwanted → negative, ubiquitous → property/monitor, optional-feature → flag matrix — and is never auto-filled.
rule.rationale: EARS has no concept of identity, priority, traceability or verification — the four things that make a requirement referenceable for the life of a product. Our layer has all four and no sentence discipline. The composition is clean because the overlap is exactly one field. The `n-a` value exists so that "not applicable" is distinguishable from "not done": calling EARS merely "advisory for NFRs" is unmeasurable, and an unmeasurable rule is an unenforced rule. Recording the opt-out as a value is the whole difference.

rule.statement: When a candidate is not a system response to a condition, EARS MUST refuse it and route it, never dress it in `shall`. Goals and outcome metrics → `roadmap.md` success metrics with a measured target. Data and domain invariants → `project-spec/`. Quality attributes stated as adjectives ("intuitive", "modern") → either rewrite into a measurable system response or drop; an unmeasurable adjective inside a `shall` sentence is worse than the prose it replaced, because it now looks checked. Spikes → no requirement at all; the output is learning.

rationale.source: Wikipedia EARS limitations section, fetched 2026-08-03; Terzakis ICCGI 2013

rule.rationale: Wikipedia's own limitations note records that EARS "suits conditional behaviour poorly for architectural constraints and non-functional requirements not expressible as system responses to conditions". Some NFRs ARE expressible — "The service shall encrypt data at rest using AES-256" is a fine ubiquitous requirement — and those should use EARS. A maximalist rollout that forces goals and invariants through the grammar is how a good notation acquires a bad reputation inside one sprint.

rule.statement: No claim made about EARS or about the linter may imply correctness. EARS makes a requirement unambiguous; it does not make it right, complete, consistent, or well-prioritised. A statement that parses clean and trips zero rules MUST still pass human or agent review against the spec's intent, and `verification_method` MUST still be populated. Set-level gaps — an `If X` requirement with no requirement covering `not X` — are invisible to a line-level linter and MUST be caught by a separate coverage pass, not assumed away.

rationale.source: dossier §Honest limits; Terzakis ICCGI 2013 boot-disk example

rule.rationale: "When a customer submits the checkout form, the payment service shall charge the customer twice." is perfect EARS: it parses, classifies event-driven, and trips zero rules. The linter is a grammar checker for requirements in exactly the sense that `gofmt` is not a type checker. Terzakis's boot-disk case — "If a boot disk is detected, the software shall boot from it. — What if a boot disk is not present? The logic is incomplete." — is the canonical demonstration that no line-level rule can see the hole. Selling the tool as more than this is a lie the first customer catches, and the positioning that survives a web search is narrow and true: QVscribe has shipped machine-validated EARS since its 2.10 release on 2019-08-21 into DOORS Next / Jama / Polarion, and `labeth/ears-lint-go` (MIT) exists — the defensible claim is "the first EARS validator that runs inside your coding agent: one binary, no seat licence", never "nobody has built this".
